title: The Body in the Canal
subtitle: Friday and Saturday: A Drowned Man Who Did Not Drink, the Back Door of the Morgue, Sixty-One Photostats

setting.name: New Orleans, Friday 1 and Saturday 2 March 1946
setting.description: The first two days of the calendar, four days before Mardi Gras. The case begins at the Industrial Canal lock at dawn and moves across the city: the 5th District station house, the coroner's office and the parish morgue in the basement of the Criminal Courts Building at Tulane and Broad, the Fontenots' half of a shotgun double on Louisa Street in the Upper Ninth Ward, Crescent Photostat Co. on Carondelet Street and the Ducros Loan Office on St. Claude Avenue, and Jourdan Avenue along the fence of Ste. Claire Marine Ways. The party may begin together at Thériot Inquiries on Decatur Street (Irene Fontenot climbs the stairs at 2 p.m. Friday) or separately: Det. Lamarque at the lock at 8:15 a.m., Wade Robichaux at the Poland Avenue shape-up at 7, Octave Mercier at the Statesman when the word comes in, Zélie Pichon at the Tremé Taxi stand, Solange Delery reading the Times-Picayune over coffee at noon.
setting.atmosphere: Steam off wet streets, the river smell, coffee and chicory. Carnival bunting going up on Canal Street balconies; children in the Ninth Ward practicing on cornets. The lock's iron gates and brown water, gulls, a tug's horn. In the Criminal Courts basement: carbolic, cold, a tin-shaded bulb, a sign over one door reading WHITE and over the other COLORED, and the porters who move between both. A widow's front room: a photograph of a young man in a straw boater, an ironing board still up. The tone is quiet and wrong: everyone official is in a hurry to be finished, and the party is the only one asking why.

keyLocations.name: The Industrial Canal Lock and the Tender's House
keyLocations.description: At the river end of the Industrial Canal, where the St. Claude Avenue bridge crosses over the lock: two pairs of steel gates, a lock chamber six hundred feet long, a brick tender's house with a telephone and a log, and the levee beside it where men fish for sac-a-lait. The body fetched up against the upper gates and was pulled out with a boat hook at 5:50 a.m.
features: The lock log: Fortuné Guidry's entries for Thursday night (two tugs and a barge at 7, 11 and 2, gates closed between) and Friday 5:45 a.m.: 'Body of white man against upper gates, telephoned police.'
The levee, where Guidry's grandson Ti-Paul fishes after dark
The canal current: slow, toward the lock when the gates are shut; anything dropped off the yards upstream comes down to the gates in a few hours
The St. Claude bridge above, with the Tremé Taxi drivers' habit of waiting at its downtown foot for fares off the Ninth Ward streetcar
encounters: Fortuné Guidry, 64, lock tender, Friday morning onward
Det. Vincent Lamarque and two patrolmen at 8:15 a.m., if he is not played; the morgue wagon at 8:40
secrets: CLUE A4 (core, automatic for anyone who talks to Guidry): 'I pulled eleven drowned men off those gates in twenty years. A drunk goes in, he sinks, he comes up in three days, swole. This one wasn't in the water four hours. And he had his wallet: eleven dollars and his yard pass. Nobody rolls a drunk and leaves him eleven dollars.' Insight DC 12: Guidry is frightened of something; he says a police captain told him on the telephone at seven 'not to make a story of it'.

CLUE B3 (core, automatic if anyone asks Guidry about Thursday night or speaks to Ti-Paul, 13, on the levee after school): Ti-Paul was fishing at about 9:20 Thursday and saw a flashlight moving on the Ste. Claire fitting-out pier, a long way up on the east bank, then heard a splash 'big as a tarpon', then the flashlight went away. He did not tell the police because nobody asked him. A Tremé Taxi driver, or Zélie Pichon, saw a long grey car come fast off Jourdan Avenue with its lights off at 9:15 (if Zélie is not played, Mr. Ulric Bazile of the Tremé Taxi Company tells whoever asks at the stand, Streetwise DC 10 or one dollar).

keyLocations.name: The Coroner's Office and the Parish Morgue, Criminal Courts Building
keyLocations.description: Tulane Avenue at Broad Street, a limestone courthouse of 1931 with the parish prison behind it. In the basement, the coroner's office (front, white staff, a counter, a deputy coroner who signs) and the morgue (back, a tiled room with eight steel tables, a cold room, and three Black porters, of whom Alcée Toussaint is the night man). The front entrance is for white visitors; the porters and Black families use the side door on Gravier Street.
features: The deputy coroner's file on Marcel Fontenot: a single sheet, 'accidental drowning, acute alcoholic intoxication', signed by Dr. Placide Faucheux at 11:40 a.m., with the boxes for autopsy, blood alcohol and stomach contents left empty
The cold room, where the body lies until Irene claims it Saturday
The side door, the porters' room, and a telephone on the wall that Alcée uses to call his sister
A wire basket of personal effects: the yard pass, the wallet, a wristwatch strap without a watch, house keys, and no notebook (Lebeau's men took it to the property room)
encounters: Dr. Placide Faucheux, deputy coroner, by day: bored, condescending, and quick to call the police if pressed
Alcée Toussaint, 29, porter, from 6 p.m.
Dr. Philomène Toussaint, whom Alcée calls at 6:30 Friday evening and who arrives by the side door at 9
secrets: CLUE A1 (core, automatic for a Doctor examining the body, for Dr. Toussaint, or for any Forensics look by a character who knows what to check for): no froth in the mouth or airways, the lungs not waterlogged, no silt in the windpipe. He did not breathe water. He was dead when he went in.

CLUE A2 (core, automatic on any examination of the head): a depressed fracture behind the left ear, two blows close together, from something heavy, flexible and narrow, like a sap or a leather-covered cosh, struck from behind by a right-handed man taller than Marcel (Dr. Toussaint's Coroner practice gives 'taller, right-handed, and he knew where to hit').

CLUE B1 (core, automatic on examining hair or clothing): flecks of red-lead primer, the orange-red paint that goes on steel hulls before the grey, and fine steel shot-blast grit in his hair and the seams of his coat. Forensics DC 12 or anyone who has worked in a yard (Wade, Theo, Octave): this comes from a fitting-out pier where hulls are blasted and painted, not from a street or a bar.

CLUE A3, coroner's half (core, automatic for anyone who reads the file): the deputy coroner took no blood and examined no stomach; the rye smell is on the coat and shirt front, and Dr. Toussaint finds none on the breath or in the mouth. Rye poured, not drunk.

Alcée kept the shirt collar, which Faucheux's assistant threw in the bin. It has red lead and a smear of brown leather dye on it at the back. He will give it to his sister; it matters in cs-scenario-004 (Clue G2's physical half).

keyLocations.name: The Fontenot Double, 2900 Block of Louisa Street
keyLocations.description: The right-hand half of a green shotgun double in the Upper Ninth Ward, a mile from the yard: front room, two bedrooms, a kitchen, a yard with a fig tree and a wash line. Irene Fontenot lives here alone now. Marcel's desk is in the second bedroom, a rolltop with a cracked slat.
features: Marcel's desk: bills, a pledge card from a temperance society dated 1931, the pawn ticket for his watch in a pigeonhole, a receipt from Crescent Photostat Co. folded inside it
His Wednesday shirt in the laundry basket, with dried paste and gold paint on the right cuff
A photograph of Marcel and Irene at Pontchartrain Beach in 1938, and a photograph of the yard's 1943 pay office staff, Irene in the front row
The back door, whose lock any professional can open, and the side alley along which Gravier's men will come
encounters: Irene Fontenot, at home after 4 p.m. Friday and all day Saturday
Gravier's men (three Dockside Goons led by Dutch Haydel, a Street Tough) at 11 p.m. Friday; see Act 3
secrets: CLUE A3, the widow's half (core, automatic if anyone asks Irene about the drink): 'He took the pledge in 1931 after his father died of it. Fifteen years. He wouldn't eat a rum cake.' The temperance card is in the desk.

CLUE B4 (core, automatic once Irene trusts the party, which is immediately if they believe her): on Thursday at a quarter past eight Marcel said he was going back to the yard at nine 'to meet the Commander, who can make the Navy listen'. She does not know who the Commander is; she thinks it is a Navy officer, an honest one. 'He said it was a man who'd been there all through the war and wanted to put it right.'

CLUE C1 (core, automatic once she trusts the party): on Wednesday night Marcel came home after midnight frightened, with paste and gold paint on his sleeve (CLUE F4, see the shirt), and told her he had taken 'the Navy copies' from the vault and that 'if anything happens they're somewhere nobody would think to look, in plain sight'. He would not tell her where, 'so you can't be made to say'. He had pawned his watch. She knows what the Navy copies are: she typed them in 1943.

CLUE C2, first half (core, automatic on searching the desk): the pawn ticket, Ducros Loan Office, St. Claude Avenue, one Hamilton wristwatch, $20, Wednesday 27 February, and a receipt from Crescent Photostat Co., 61 sheets at 30 cents, $18.30, the same date.

CLUE C3 (core, automatic once it happens): at 11 p.m. Friday Gravier's men break in by the back door to search for the papers (Act 3). If the party is not here, Irene comes home from a neighbour's at midnight to find the desk emptied onto the floor, the mattresses slit and the icebox open, and telephones the agency. Nothing of value is taken. Someone is looking for papers, and has not found them.

Irene's own secret, which she tells only if asked why she is so sure Marcel was killed for the papers: in 1943 she typed two sets of pay summaries every week, one for the yard's own books and one 'Navy copy', and the Navy copy had a hundred and forty more names on it, all on gang No. 9, and the Black welders were listed as Welders First Class. She asked Marcel about it once. He told her not to ask. She left the yard in 1944. She has been ashamed of it ever since, and she pushed him in January to 'do something about those poor men put out at the gate'. She believes it is her fault he is dead.

keyLocations.name: Crescent Photostat Co., Carondelet Street, and the Ducros Loan Office, St. Claude Avenue
keyLocations.description: Two small businesses Marcel visited on Wednesday 27 February. Crescent Photostat is a narrow shop in the business district with two big photostat cameras, a darkroom and a counter, open until 7 p.m., where lawyers and title companies have documents copied. The Ducros Loan Office is a pawnshop on St. Claude Avenue in the Ninth Ward with three gold balls over the door and Mr. Hilaire Ducros behind a grille.
features: Crescent Photostat's order book: 'Wed 2/27, cash, 61 sh., L.F.' in Mrs. Hingle's hand
The photostat negatives, which the shop keeps for thirty days and Mrs. Hingle could reprint for $18.30 (a bonus route to Clue D2 if the party thinks of it: the reprints are ready Monday morning)
At Ducros's: Marcel's Hamilton watch, engraved 'L.F. from I.F. 1934', in the window case
encounters: Mrs. Myrtle Hingle, 50s, photostat clerk, sharp-eyed and chatty
Mr. Hilaire Ducros, 60s, pawnbroker, deaf in one ear and discreet in both
secrets: CLUE C2, second half (core, automatic if the party asks at either shop): Mrs. Hingle remembers him because he was so nervous: 'Sixty-one sheets of Navy forms, pay summaries, columns of names, and a ledger of envelopes. He watched every sheet go through and paid in cash out of an envelope. He said he was a clerk taking his work home.' Ducros remembers that he pawned his wedding-present watch for $20 and asked twice whether it would be safe until Saturday week.

Persuasion DC 13 or $5: Mrs. Hingle adds that on Friday afternoon a large polite man with a Navy ring telephoned to ask whether a Mr. Fontenot had had any copying done, and she said she did not discuss customers' business. (It was Pruett, checking whether more copies exist. He did not ask about negatives. If the party does not order the reprints, nobody does.)

keyLocations.name: Jourdan Avenue and the Ste. Claire Gatehouse
keyLocations.description: Jourdan Avenue runs along the east side of the Industrial Canal past the yards' fences. Ste. Claire Marine Ways' gate is a chain-link double gate with a gatehouse, a turnstile for workers on foot and a counter where the night watchman keeps the night-pass log. At night there is one watchman, Clovis Pinac, 66, Honoré Ste. Claire's man for forty years.
features: Marcel's 1937 Plymouth sedan, parked on Jourdan Avenue two hundred yards from the gate, outside the fence
The gatehouse, with the night-pass log on its counter and a telephone to the Esplanade house
Behind the fence: the building ways, the crane on the fitting-out pier, the long roof of the mold loft with light in its windows until midnight, where the floats are being finished
encounters: Clovis Pinac, the night watchman (Night Watchman stats) and his dog, Bijou (Guard Dog)
A 5th District patrol car that passes every hour
secrets: CLUE B2 (core, automatic on looking at the car, and on looking at the log): the Plymouth's driver's seat is pushed back for a taller man than Marcel, and its tires carry the yard's crushed oyster-shell gravel. The night-pass log's Thursday page has been torn out; Investigation DC 10 (or holding the next page to the light, no roll) reads the pencil impression on the Friday page: 'FONTENOT PLYM IN 20:40', no OUT; 'L. STE. C. CADILLAC IN 18:10 OUT 21:12'; 'CMDR PRUETT (on foot) IN 18:30'.

Pinac moved the car at 6:30 Friday morning and tore out the page on Honoré's order. He will not admit it in cs-scenario-001 (Deception +2 against Insight; on a success the party knows he is lying and is frightened for his employer, not himself). He breaks in cs-scenario-003 or 004 (Clue H2).
The pencil impression is the first appearance of 'the Commander' as a name: CMDR PRUETT. The party may not know who he is until cs-scenario-002.

keyLocations.name: Thériot Inquiries, 1019 Decatur Street, Upstairs
keyLocations.description: One room over Broussard's shoe repair in the lower French Quarter, a desk from a bankrupt dentist, two chairs for clients, a hat rack, a telephone, a window over the street and the smell of leather and polish from below. The agency's whole capital is Remy Thériot's GI Bill loan. If Remy is not played, use it as the party's office anyway: Irene found the advertisement.
features: A blackboard bought from a closed school: the case board
The telephone, a party line shared with the shoe repair, and Mr. Broussard listens
The window, from which a parked Buick with two men in it can be seen from Saturday morning
encounters: Irene Fontenot, Friday 2 p.m.: the client
Prosper Vidrine, attorney, Saturday 10 a.m.: the other client
secrets: CLUE C4 (core, automatic when Vidrine visits): Prosper Vidrine, of Vidrine, Hebert and Lalande on Carondelet Street, attorney for the Ste. Claire family, offers the party $500 to 'recover company payroll records removed without authority by the late Mr. Fontenot, and to treat the matter in confidence'. He names no family member; Insight DC 12 shows he is frightened of the client, and has been told not to say who. Society DC 12 or any Old Money character knows the firm is the Ste. Claires'. He leaves a card and $100 'for your trouble' on the desk whatever the answer.
The men in the Buick from Saturday are Lebeau's plainclothesmen if Heat is 3 or more, Gravier's if it is not.

synopsis: At dawn on Friday 1 March the lock tender at the Industrial Canal finds Marcel Fontenot, pay clerk at Ste. Claire Marine Ways, dead against the lock gates. By noon Captain Achille Lebeau of the 5th District has ruled it an accidental drowning of a drunk, and the deputy coroner has signed it without looking. Irene Fontenot hires the party at 2 p.m. with sixty dollars and the certainty that her husband, a teetotaler for fifteen years, did not fall into a canal drunk. Over two days the party learns, from the lock tender, from a Black physician and her brother at the back door of the parish morgue, and from the widow herself, that Marcel was beaten to death with a sap and put into the canal from the Ste. Claire yard's fitting-out pier on Thursday night, after going there to meet 'the Commander'; that he had taken the Navy copies of the yard's pay summaries from its vault on Wednesday and had sixty-one pages photostatted; and that someone is hunting for them: men search the widow's house on Friday night, and on Saturday the family's lawyer offers the party five hundred dollars to bring them in. By Saturday night the party knows it was murder, where it happened, and that it was about papers. They do not yet know what the papers prove, who the Commander is, or where Marcel hid them.
hook: Friday 1 March 1946, two o'clock in the afternoon, Decatur Street. The shoe repair downstairs is hammering. There are four days to Mardi Gras and someone across the street is hanging purple and gold bunting from a balcony and dropping it. A woman comes up the stairs slowly: thirty-six, small, in a black dress that does not quite fit her, borrowed, with a straw hat and white cotton gloves, and in one gloved hand a newspaper advertisement folded very small. She sits when asked and does not cry. She puts sixty dollars on the desk, in ones and fives, and says that her name is Irene Fontenot, that her husband Marcel was taken out of the Industrial Canal this morning, and that the police have told her he fell in drunk. 'My husband had not had a drink since 1931,' she says. 'He would not eat a rum cake. I want to know who killed him. That is all the money I have.'

conclusions.conclusion: A. Marcel Fontenot was murdered, not drowned drunk
clues: A1: no water in the lungs (the morgue, Dr. Toussaint)
A2: two blows behind the left ear from a sap (the morgue)
A3: rye poured on his coat and none in him; a teetotaler since 1931; no blood or stomach sample taken (the morgue and the Fontenot house)
A4: in the water a few hours, wallet still holding $11 (the lock tender)

conclusions.conclusion: B. He was killed at Ste. Claire Marine Ways on Thursday night
clues: B1: red-lead primer and shot-blast grit in his hair and coat (the morgue)
B2: his car moved out of the yard, the gate log's torn page showing him IN at 20:40 and no OUT (Jourdan Avenue, the gatehouse)
B3: the flashlight and the splash off the fitting-out pier at 9:20; a grey car leaving with its lights off at 9:15 (the lock levee; the Tremé Taxi stand)
B4: he told Irene he was going to the yard at nine to meet 'the Commander' (the Fontenot house)

conclusions.conclusion: C. He took papers from the yard, and someone wants them badly
clues: C1: Irene: 'the Navy copies' from the vault, hidden 'in plain sight' (the Fontenot house)
C2: the pawn ticket and the photostat receipt; Mrs. Hingle's sixty-one sheets of Navy pay forms (Carondelet Street, St. Claude Avenue)
C3: Gravier's men search the house on Friday night (the Fontenot house)
C4: the Ste. Claires' lawyer offers $500 for 'company payroll records' (the agency office)

acts.title: Act 1: Against the Lock Gates
acts.description: Friday morning to early afternoon. The party comes together over the body, either because Irene hires them, because Det. Lamarque has caught the case and does not like his captain's verdict, or because each of them has a reason to care (Wade knew Marcel; Octave knows what Marcel did at the yard; Zélie saw the grey car; Solange saw Lucien Ste. Claire white as paper at the Isabeau). The act is about the city's indifference and the first wrong notes. About an hour of play.
objectives: Learn how the body was found and what the lock tender thinks
Hear the official verdict, and notice how fast it came
Take the case from Irene Fontenot

scenes.name: Gates
scenes.description: At the lock, any time Friday. Guidry tells the party what he told the police and what he did not (A4). If Lamarque is played, he arrives at 8:15 with two patrolmen and the morgue wagon is called; if he is not, the party arrives after the police have gone and finds Guidry still shaken, and his grandson on the levee after 3 p.m. (B3).
scenes.readAloud: The lock is a long concrete trough of brown water between the river and the canal, with iron gates at each end as tall as a house and a brick tender's house beside it with geraniums in a coffee can. Above it the St. Claude Avenue bridge carries streetcars and trucks across, and every few minutes it shakes. An old man in a rubber apron is hosing down the walk beside the upper gates, slowly, over and over, as if there were something on it that would not come off. Gulls sit on the gate beams. Up the canal, on the east bank, you can see the cranes and the long roofs of the shipyards, quiet now, and a tug pushing a barge with nobody in a hurry.

skillChecks.success: Guidry is not grieving; he is afraid. When pressed gently he says that a police captain telephoned him at seven, before anyone had told him who the dead man was, and told him not to 'make a story of it'. He has a pension coming in two years.
skillChecks.failure: An old man upset by a drowning. He tells you what he knows and wants you to go.

skillChecks.success: From where the body lay and the slack current with the gates shut, it went in upstream on the east bank within the last six or eight hours: somewhere around the yards. (This confirms B3 and points at B1.)
skillChecks.failure: The canal does not tell you anything you can use.

skillChecks.success: At the downtown foot of the bridge, the Tremé Taxi drivers who wait for the Ninth Ward streetcar say one of their own saw a big grey car with no lights coming off Jourdan Avenue at a quarter past nine last night 'like the devil was driving it'. That is Zélie Pichon, or Ulric Bazile (B3).
skillChecks.failure: The cab drivers look at you, and at each other, and say they did not see anything. A white stranger asking questions about a white man's death on the canal is trouble they do not need. (A Black or Creole character, or Zélie herself, gets the answer without a roll.)

scenes.name: The Captain's Accident
scenes.description: At the 5th District station house, late morning. Captain Achille Lebeau, fifty-eight, heavy, silver-haired, a rosary of Carnival invitations on his desk, tells Lamarque (or any visitor with a reason to ask) that it is an accidental drowning and that he will hear no more about it in Carnival week. He is genial, final and quick to threaten. This scene establishes that the official verdict came before the evidence. If Lamarque is played, Lebeau orders him to type it up and gives him the parade detail for Tuesday night; Lamarque has typed it and not yet signed it.
scenes.readAloud: Captain Lebeau's office has a window onto the parking yard, a portrait of the mayor, a framed photograph of the captain shaking hands with a man in a Carnival king's crown, and a desk stacked with engraved envelopes. The captain is a large, pink, silver-haired man in a beautiful grey suit, and he does not get up. 'Pay clerk,' he says. 'Forty-one years old. Smelled like a distillery. Walked off a wharf in the dark. It happens every Carnival, it'll happen fifty times before Wednesday, and I don't have the men to hold a hand for every one.' He smiles. 'It's Carnival, son. Let the man's widow bury him.'

skillChecks.success: He decided before anyone told him anything. He has not seen the coroner's report; he is quoting what he expects it to say. And he is uneasy, not about the dead man but about whoever he is doing this for.
skillChecks.failure: A busy, lazy captain with a city full of drunks to manage.

skillChecks.success: On the switchboard sergeant's log by the front desk, a line for 6:10 a.m. Friday: an incoming call for the captain at home, put through 'from Esplanade'. (A bonus route to Clue H1 for cs-scenario-003 and 004; the party may not understand it yet.)
skillChecks.failure: The front desk is busy and the sergeant shoos you out.

scenes.name: Sixty Dollars
scenes.description: Irene Fontenot hires the party at 2 p.m. at the agency (see the hook). She has sixty dollars and wants the truth. She does not want revenge; she wants his name. This is the emotional anchor of the campaign: play her as plain, intelligent, contained and stubborn, and let her say very little. If the party is mixed, she is polite to everyone and visibly unsure how to treat Octave, Theo or Zélie, and then decides, and that small decision should be visible. She invites them to the house at 4.
scenes.readAloud: She sits very straight with her gloves in her lap and looks at each of you in turn, the way you look at a plumber before you let him into the house. 'The police say he was drinking at a bar on the canal and walked off a wharf,' she says. 'Marcel took the pledge the year his father died of it. He had not touched a drop in fifteen years. He used to say a drink was the only thing in life he was sure he could do without.' She opens her purse and takes out an envelope and counts sixty dollars onto the desk, in ones and fives, and squares them. 'I am not asking you to get anybody,' she says. 'I am asking you to find out. Then I will know what to do.'

skillChecks.success: She is telling the truth, and she is carrying something besides grief: guilt. She thinks she is in some way responsible.
skillChecks.failure: She is in shock and holding it together by force of will.

skillChecks.success: She tells you now, rather than at the house, about the Commander (B4) and that Marcel said 'if anything happens, they're in plain sight'.
skillChecks.failure: She says she will tell you everything at the house, where his things are.

encounters: Fortuné Guidry, lock tender (no combat)
Captain Achille Lebeau (no combat; Police Captain if it ever comes to that, which it should not)
Irene Fontenot, the client (no combat)

acts.title: Act 2: What the Coroner Did Not Look At
acts.description: Friday afternoon to late Friday night. Three places, each with core clues: the Fontenot house (A3, B4, C1, C2, F4), the morgue (A1, A2, A3, B1), and Jourdan Avenue and the gatehouse (B2). Crescent Photostat and the pawnshop (C2) can be visited until 7 p.m. Friday or on Saturday morning. The morgue can be reached two ways: by the front door, where Dr. Faucheux refuses everything and calls the police if pushed (Heat +1); or by the side door after 6 p.m., where Alcée Toussaint and his sister Dr. Philomène Toussaint examine the body properly for the first time. The side door is the better route and it is a Black route: Alcée will open it for Octave, Theo, Zélie or anyone Philomène vouches for, or for a white character who comes with one of them and treats him as a colleague. He will not open it for a policeman alone.
objectives: Examine the body, or have someone competent do it
Search Marcel's desk and hear what Irene knows
Find Marcel's car and the yard's gate log
Trace the pawn ticket and the photostat receipt

scenes.name: The Side Door on Gravier Street
scenes.description: Friday from 9 p.m. in the morgue. Dr. Philomène Toussaint examines Marcel Fontenot under a tin-shaded bulb while her brother keeps watch on the front corridor. She does it quickly and exactly, dictating to whoever will write, and finds A1, A2 and B1 automatically. She explains plainly why she is doing it: in the last two years the coroner's office has signed forty-one Black deaths as accidents without opening the body, and she has a list; this is the first time she has seen them do it to a white man, and if she can prove it here, the list becomes a question the newspapers have to ask. She wants the party's word that her findings will be used and her list printed with them. A Doctor in the party can assist and confirm everything. Halfway through, the night supervisor, a white clerk named Mr. Aurelien Thibaut, comes down the stairs for his coffee: the party must hide, bluff or brazen it (Deception or Stealth DC 13; if caught, Heat +1 and Alcée is suspended without pay unless someone talks fast).
scenes.readAloud: The morgue is colder than the night outside and smells of carbolic and wet stone. Eight steel tables, seven of them empty, and on the eighth, under a sheet, a man. Dr. Toussaint folds the sheet down to his chest as carefully as if he were asleep, says quietly 'Good evening, Mr. Fontenot,' and puts on her spectacles. Her brother stands at the corridor door with his hand on the light switch. She opens the dead man's mouth, looks, and is silent for a moment. Then she looks up at you over her spectacles. 'Write this down, please,' she says. 'Somebody ought to have written it down this morning.'

skillChecks.success: Bonus detail: bruising on the right wrist where someone held him, and a torn thumbnail with something under it, a fibre of navy-blue wool serge, the cloth of a naval officer's uniform or a good blue suit. (A pointer toward Pruett for later.)
skillChecks.failure: The core findings are Dr. Toussaint's anyway; you miss the wrist and the thumbnail.

skillChecks.success: Time of death between eight and eleven on Thursday night, from the state of the body and the cold of the water.
skillChecks.failure: Some time Thursday night.

skillChecks.success: Dr. Toussaint, satisfied that the party means it, tells you about her list and asks you to come and see it at Flint-Goodridge. She will be your doctor for the rest of the case. (She joins as a companion.)
skillChecks.failure: She does her work, gives you her findings, and tells you she will believe in you when she sees what you do with them.

scenes.name: Louisa Street
scenes.description: The Fontenot house, Friday from 4 p.m. or any time Saturday. Irene shows the party Marcel's desk and tells them everything she knows (A3, B4, C1, F4), and the desk gives the pawn ticket and the photostat receipt (C2). She tells her own secret (that she typed the Navy copies) if asked why she is sure it was the papers. The scene should be quiet, close and sad. Neighbours come by with food. A radio next door plays Carnival songs.
scenes.readAloud: The front room is very clean. There is an ironing board still up in the corner with a man's white shirt half-pressed on it, and nobody has moved it. On the wall, a framed marriage certificate and a photograph of a young man in a straw boater, laughing, with his arm around a girl who is Irene twenty years younger. She shows you into the back bedroom, where a rolltop desk with a cracked slat stands under the window, and then she stands in the doorway with her arms folded and watches you open her husband's drawers, and does not say anything at all.

skillChecks.success: Core finds as listed, plus: in the back of the desk, an empty bank envelope from the yard's pay office marked BONUS L.F. 25.00 in red pencil, and twelve more like it, folded flat, three years of Fridays. Marcel was being paid to keep quiet, and kept the envelopes. (Follow the Money, or Insight with Irene: he kept them the way a man keeps a sin in his pocket.)
skillChecks.failure: You find the pawn ticket and receipt and nothing else of use.

skillChecks.success: The laundry basket: a shirt with a right cuff stiff with dried flour paste and specks of gold paint (F4). Not from a pay office.
skillChecks.failure: Irene mentions the paste on his sleeve herself if asked about Wednesday.

skillChecks.success: Irene is holding back something that shames her. Asked kindly, she tells you about typing the two sets of summaries in 1943.
skillChecks.failure: She has told you what she thinks you need. She will tell the rest when she trusts you more.

scenes.name: A Plymouth on Jourdan Avenue
scenes.description: Friday evening or night, at the yard fence. Marcel's car (B2) is parked outside the fence where no clerk would leave it. The gatehouse is lit; Clovis Pinac and his dog Bijou are inside. The party can talk to Pinac (who lies), read the night-pass log (the torn page and its impression, B2), or slip past him into the yard (Stealth DC 13 against his passive Perception; Bijou has advantage; Heat +2 if seen). Inside, the fitting-out pier is dark, but a GM may allow a character who goes there now to find, by flashlight, a rye bottle lid in the oyster shells at the pier's edge (bonus) and a scuff of blood on the timber that a rain has nearly washed out.
scenes.readAloud: Jourdan Avenue is dark and empty, a road of oyster shell and puddles along a chain-link fence, and beyond the fence the shipyard is a black geometry of cranes and staging against the glow of the city. A long low building near the water has every window lit and you can hear, very faintly, hammering and somebody singing. Two hundred yards short of the gatehouse a grey Plymouth sedan stands alone under a dead streetlight, as if somebody had stopped there to change a tire and walked away. Nobody has bothered to lock it.

skillChecks.success: The log's Friday page carries the impression of the torn Thursday page: FONTENOT PLYM IN 20:40, no OUT; L. STE. C. CADILLAC IN 18:10 OUT 21:12; CMDR PRUETT (on foot) IN 18:30 (B2).
skillChecks.failure: The Thursday page is gone, torn out raggedly. The impression is still there for the next person who thinks to look, or for anyone with a pencil and the patience to shade it.

skillChecks.success: Pinac is lying to protect someone he loves more than himself: an employer. He looks at the telephone on the wall, the one to Esplanade Avenue, every time you ask him a question.
skillChecks.failure: An old man who does not want trouble.

skillChecks.success: The Plymouth's engine was cold by midnight Thursday, but its seat is pushed back three notches and there is oyster-shell gravel from the yard lot packed in the treads. Someone drove it out of the yard this morning and walked back.
skillChecks.failure: An old car with a flat-ish rear tire. Nothing more.

encounters: Mr. Aurelien Thibaut, night supervisor at the morgue (no combat; a bluff or a hiding place)
Clovis Pinac (Night Watchman) and Bijou (Guard Dog), only if the party breaks into the yard
A 5th District patrol car (2 Beat Cops) on Jourdan Avenue at the top of each hour

acts.title: Act 3: Friday Night, Saturday Morning
acts.description: The opposition shows its hand. At 11 p.m. Friday, Emile Gravier's men search the Fontenot house for the papers. If the party is there, it is a fight or a chase; if not, Irene comes home from a neighbour's to find the house torn apart and telephones the agency. On Saturday morning Prosper Vidrine comes to the agency with $500. On Saturday afternoon Irene claims the body for burial on Monday. The scenario ends when the party has reached conclusions A, B and C and knows that the papers exist, that they were not found, and that the Ste. Claire family is paying to get them back.
objectives: Survive, stop or follow the men who search the house
Hear Vidrine's offer, and decide what to say
Decide where to look next: the yard, the Navy, or the men Marcel worked with

scenes.name: Men in the House
scenes.description: Friday 11 p.m. Dutch Haydel (Street Tough with 15 hit points and a sap) and three Dockside Goons come down the side alley and in by the back door with a crowbar. They are not murderers; they have orders to find papers, frighten the widow and leave. If the party is in the house it is a fistfight in a shotgun house, room to room, with an ironing board, a fig tree and a wash line; Haydel runs at half his men down, toward a Ford truck on the next street. Caught and leaned on (Intimidation DC 12, or The Look), a goon says they work for Gravier, that 'the boss's boss' wants some papers 'that the clerk stole', and that they were told to leave the widow alone 'unless she screamed'. Wade Robichaux knows Haydel: they boxed in 1940. If nobody is there, the house is wrecked and the desk's pigeonholes emptied onto the floor, and the pawn ticket is gone unless the party already took it (Clue C3 either way).
scenes.readAloud: The back door goes with the flat crack of a crowbar and a man's voice says, too loudly, 'Nobody home, he said.' Then flashlights: three, four of them, sweeping the kitchen, the icebox, the calendar from the Ninth Ward grocery, and somebody knocks a chair over and swears. Heavy men in caps and dock jackets, one of them with a sap in his fist and a face you would not want to meet twice. They have not seen you yet.

skillChecks.success: A captured goon gives up Gravier's name, the 'boss's boss', and the order to find 'a box of Navy papers, about yea big'. He also says, unasked, that nobody told them to touch the clerk, and that Gravier was angry on Friday morning when he heard the clerk was dead.
skillChecks.failure: He says nothing but his name, which is Mouton, and spits.

skillChecks.success: Instead of fighting, you follow them: the Ford truck goes to the Gravier Stevedoring wharf at the foot of Poland Avenue, where a light is on in an upstairs office and a big man in shirtsleeves takes a telephone call from someone he calls 'Mr. Lucien'. (A bonus route to Gravier and to Lucien.)
skillChecks.failure: They see the tail at the canal and lose you on the St. Claude bridge; Heat +1.

scenes.name: The Other Client
scenes.description: Saturday 10 a.m. at the agency. Prosper Vidrine, forty, plump, perfectly dressed, a Carnival lapel pin in purple and green, makes the $500 offer (C4) and leaves $100 on the desk regardless. He is a decent man in a bad job: he does not know about the murder and does not want to. If the party asks who the client is, he says 'a respected family' and looks at the floor. If they refuse, he says 'I would think carefully, gentlemen. There are people in this city who do not take refusals graciously, and I am not one of them.' If the party accepts, they have taken the Ste. Claires' money, which will matter when Theo Dorsainville asks who they are working for.
scenes.readAloud: He knocks, which nobody does, and comes in with his hat in his hand and his umbrella furled, and stands for a moment looking at the blackboard as if it might be rude to read it. Then he puts a card on the desk: PROSPER M. VIDRINE, ATTORNEY AT LAW, CARONDELET STREET. 'I represent a family,' he says, 'who employed the late Mr. Fontenot, and who were distressed to learn of his death, and more distressed to learn that certain business records left the premises with him on Wednesday.' He takes out an envelope. 'Five hundred dollars,' he says, 'for their return. No questions. And this,' a second, thinner envelope, 'for your time this morning.'

skillChecks.success: He is afraid of his client, and ashamed of this errand. He does not know Marcel was murdered and his hand shakes when you tell him.
skillChecks.failure: A smooth lawyer doing a smooth lawyer's job.

skillChecks.success: Vidrine, Hebert and Lalande have been the Ste. Claire family's lawyers for forty years. (Any Old Money character, or Solange, knows this without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: A Carondelet Street firm like fifty others.

scenes.name: Where Next
scenes.description: Saturday afternoon and evening: the case board scene. Irene claims the body at 2 p.m. (the funeral is Monday morning). The party should now be able to say: he was murdered, at the yard, for papers that are still missing and that the Ste. Claires want. Open threads point three ways: the yard itself (B2, the Commander's name on the gate log), the Navy (Marcel called them; 'the Commander'), and the yard's Black welders (Octave's sixty-one names; Irene's 'those poor men put out at the gate'). If Octave is not played, Dr. Toussaint or Irene points the party to Theo Dorsainville and the Equity Benevolent Association: 'Marcel went to see a colored man on North Roman Street last Monday. He said it was the most important thing he had ever done.' End with a quiet beat: Solange (or a bartender at the Isabeau, if she is not played) remembering Lucien Ste. Claire drinking four doubles in silence at 11:30 Thursday night (Clue H4 can come later).
scenes.readAloud: By Saturday evening the city has started its party without you. Bands are practicing in every hall in the Ninth Ward, there are children in crepe-paper crowns on the banquettes, and on Canal Street the department stores have put up the purple, green and gold. In your office the blackboard is full: a drowned man who was not drowned, a pier, a torn page, a commander, sixty-one sheets of Navy paper, and the name of a family that owns half the riverfront. Somewhere in the city those papers are lying where a frightened clerk put them, in plain sight. And three days from now the whole city puts on a mask.

skillChecks.success: A morning at the Times-Picayune's public files or the Statesman's morgue: Ste. Claire Marine Ways built lighters and tugs for the Navy on cost-plus contracts through the war, laid off most of its workers in January, and is reported to be selling to a Chicago firm 'pending settlement of its government accounts'. Its founder, Honoré Ste. Claire, was Captain of the Krewe of Oneiros from 1911 to 1936. (Octave's The Morgue gives it without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: The papers give you a yard, a family and a lot of Carnival photographs.

encounters: Dutch Haydel (Street Tough, 15 hp, sap as Blackjack) and three Dockside Goons, the Fontenot house, Friday 11 p.m.
Prosper Vidrine, attorney (no combat)

npcsInvolved.name: Irene Fontenot, 36
npcsInvolved.description: Small, plain, contained, intelligent, a former yard typist who now takes in sewing. Borrowed black dress, white cotton gloves. Says little and means all of it. Carries a guilt she has not yet named: she typed the Navy copies in 1943, and she pushed Marcel in January to 'do something about those men'.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Marcel's name. Not revenge, the truth: 'Then I will know what to do.'

npcsInvolved.name: Fortuné Guidry, 64
npcsInvolved.role: Lock tender at the Industrial Canal
npcsInvolved.description: Rubber apron, a face like a walnut, twenty years on the lock. Frightened by a captain's telephone call and ashamed of being frightened.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His pension, in two years; and, underneath it, decency.

npcsInvolved.name: Ti-Paul Guidry, 13
npcsInvolved.role: The lock tender's grandson; the witness nobody asked
npcsInvolved.description: Skinny, barefoot, a cane pole and a coffee can of shrimp. Fishes the levee every night. Proud to be asked.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be taken seriously, and a quarter.

npcsInvolved.name: Captain Achille Lebeau, 58
npcsInvolved.description: Large, pink, silver-haired, a beautiful grey suit and Carnival invitations on his desk. Genial menace. Has taken Honoré Ste. Claire's money for twenty years. Use Police Captain.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get through Carnival, keep the Ste. Claires happy, and never have to know what he is covering.

npcsInvolved.name: Dr. Placide Faucheux, 50s
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, bored, a bow tie, a fountain pen and no curiosity. Signs what the police tell him to sign. He has signed forty-one of Dr. Toussaint's cases.

npcsInvolved.name: Alcée Toussaint, 29
npcsInvolved.role: Night porter at the parish morgue; Dr. Toussaint's brother
npcsInvolved.description: A Dillard graduate in chemistry who moves bodies for the parish because it is the job he could get. Quiet, observant, funny when safe, and risking his job by opening the side door.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His sister's list, and his own self-respect; and not losing the job.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Myrtle Hingle, 50s
npcsInvolved.description: Sharp eyes, a pencil behind her ear, a Mardi Gras pin on her cardigan. Remembers every customer who was nervous.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A good story to tell her sister, and not getting into trouble.

npcsInvolved.name: Clovis Pinac, 66
npcsInvolved.role: Night watchman at Ste. Claire Marine Ways
npcsInvolved.description: Bent, white-moustached, loyal to Honoré Ste. Claire for forty years, with a dog named Bijou. Lying, badly, to protect his employer's son. Use Night Watchman.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Loyalty to the old man; fear for the young one.

npcsInvolved.name: Prosper Vidrine, 40
npcsInvolved.role: Attorney for the Ste. Claire family
npcsInvolved.description: Plump, beautifully dressed, decent and frightened, with a Carnival pin in his lapel. Offers $500 for the papers.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To do his errand and not learn what it is for.

npcsInvolved.name: Dutch Haydel, 35
npcsInvolved.description: Ex-prizefighter, flattened face, a sap in his fist, boxed Wade Robichaux in 1940 and lost. Use Street Tough with 15 hit points.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Do the job, get paid, do not go to jail for a dead clerk he did not kill.

rewards.money: Irene Fontenot's $60 retainer (split as the party likes and add each share to the wallet line). Prosper Vidrine leaves $100 on the desk whatever the party says; taking his $500 offer is possible, and the GM should remember it. About $20 between Haydel's men if anyone goes through their pockets.
items: Dr. Toussaint's written findings, signed, and her request that they be used (Clues A1, A2, B1)
Marcel's pawn ticket and the photostat receipt (Clue C2), and possibly his Hamilton watch, redeemed for $20
A rubbing of the gate log's impressed page: FONTENOT IN 20:40, L. STE. C. CADILLAC OUT 21:12, CMDR PRUETT IN 18:30 (Clue B2)
If the photostat negatives were thought of: an order for reprints, ready Monday morning at Crescent Photostat ($18.30)

twists: The official verdict came first. Captain Lebeau ruled the death an accident at 7 a.m. by telephone to the lock tender, before his own detective had reached the lock to identify the body and nearly five hours before the coroner signed. That is the first loose thread of the cover-up (Clue H1 comes from the station's switchboard log, which the party may glimpse now and understand later).

The widow is the conscience of the case and also its first cause: she typed the Navy copies in 1943 and pushed Marcel to act in January. She thinks she killed him. She did not; the man he trusted did.

Gravier's men are not the killers and say so. They were sent to find papers, which means that whoever sent them does not have the papers either. That is the first sign that more than one person is hunting and that they are not working together.

The best evidence in the scenario comes through the side door of the morgue, from two Black professionals the official city treats as furniture, and they have their own case to make. If the party uses their findings and forgets their list, Dr. Toussaint will not forget it.
The name CMDR PRUETT on the gate log looks like just another name on the night of the murder. It is the killer's, written in the watchman's hand, and the watchman tore it out to protect someone else.
dmTips: This scenario establishes the city, the client and the color line. Budget about an hour for Act 1, ninety minutes for Act 2 and an hour for Act 3. The only expected fight is the house search, and the party can avoid it or follow the men instead.

Let the city be busy and indifferent. It is four days to the first Mardi Gras since 1941 and nobody official wants a murder. Every bureaucrat the party meets is in a hurry to be finished; that hurry is the clue.

The side door of the morgue is the heart of Act 2. Play Dr. Toussaint and Alcée as professionals doing a dangerous thing for their own reasons, not as helpers. If the party includes no Black or Creole character and has not yet met Octave or Theo, let Irene send them: 'There's a colored lady doctor who looks at the ones the coroner won't, Marcel said.' A white character who comes to the side door must ask, not demand.

Show the color line in small concrete things, not speeches: the two doors, the hack licence, the streetcar screen, the way Lebeau talks to Octave, the way a cab driver will not answer a white stranger. Never make it a dice penalty, and never play it for comedy. If a player asks why something is so, a companion can tell them.
Irene is quiet. Resist making her melodramatic. One plain line from her should land harder than any speech: 'He would not eat a rum cake.'

If the party breaks into the yard on Friday night, let them reach the fitting-out pier and see where it happened (blood on the timber, the rye cap) but keep them out of the mold loft: Pichon's men are working late and will see them, and the floats are a cs-scenario-002 discovery.
If the party takes Vidrine's $500, they are now on the Ste. Claires' payroll, and the GM should let that be known at the worst moment, for instance when Theo asks who is paying them.

Track Heat openly from the start. The likeliest rises are the morgue (front door, +1), the yard at night (+2 if seen), and the fight at the house (+2 if the neighbours call the police, which they do if it reaches the street).
